ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study complies with the requirements of the Health Research Act and the Declaration of Helsinki and has been approved by the Blinded for per-review (No.).
Participants assigned to the intervention condition will have immediate access to a four-week online positive body image self-help programme designed for women in the postpartum period.
Participants are asked to complete a reflective writing task.
Participants are asked to focus on their body, notice its sensations, reflect in writing on its needs, and choose and engage in an activity that provides care, comfort, or pleasure for their body.
Participants are asked to read psychoeducational material on self-acceptance and flexibility in body image and complete a short knowledge test.
Body gratitude mindfulness meditation Participants are asked to engage in a guided mindfulnessbased meditation focused on developing gratitude towards their body.
Participants are asked to identify personal values relating to their body, reflect on how these values are expressed in their life, and formulate a positive statement about their body.
Participants are asked to reflect on factors that negatively influence their body image, and to write down at least three actions they can take to protect and strengthen it.

Adjusting to body changes in the postpartum period Participants are asked to reflect on body changes after childbirth, explore their thoughts and feelings about these changes, and then write down any positive or meaningful aspects associated with them.
Participants are asked to observe their body in a mirror without judgment, select a body part that they find difficult to accept, and express appreciation or gratitude towards it.

Self-and body acceptance mindfulness-based meditation Participants are asked to complete a guided mindfulnessbased meditation aimed at promoting relaxation and acceptance of the self and body, followed by reflection on their experience.

Participants are asked to review psychoeducational content and practical advice on maintaining a positive body image, and to apply practical strategies (e.g., self-compassion, focusing on body functionality, mindful social media use, and revisiting previously learned exercises).
Participants completed the baseline assessment (T0), the 4-week intervention, and the post-intervention assessment (T1).

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: A priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power (version 3.1.9.6; Faul et al., 2007) to determine the required sample size for this study. Given that brief digital psychological interventions typically yield small-to-moderate effects (Groot et al., 2023), the analysis was based on an effect size of f = 0.15, with α set at 0.05 and statistical power at 0.80. To approximate the planned linear mixed-effects model, the sample size calculation was conducted using the repeated-measures ANOVA within-between interaction option. The calculation was performed for two groups, two measurement points, an assumed correlation of 0.50 between repeated measures, and a nonsphericity correction of 1, indicating a required total sample size of 90 participants. To account for an anticipated attrition rate of approximately 25-35%, which is common in digital intervention studies (Linardon & Fuller-Tyszkiewicz, 2020), the target sample size was increased to 140 participants, with 70 women allocated to each group. The sample size was determined based on the primary intervention-effectiveness analysis. Mediation analyses are secondary and will be interpreted as exploratory, as the study was not specifically powered to detect indirect effects.

text.text: The high prevalence of body image concerns during the transition to motherhood underscores the need for theory-driven, accessible interventions that promote positive body image, reduce body dissatisfaction, and enhance women's resilience to unrealistic appearance ideals.
This paper presents the protocol for a two-arm randomized controlled trial (RCT) evaluating the effectiveness of BODYPOSI, a four-week digital self-help program based on positive body image theory.
The trial will include women between 6 weeks and 12 months postpartum, who will be randomly assigned to either the intervention or a waitlist control group.

Primary outcomes will include body appreciation, body functionality appreciation, appearance and weight satisfaction, evaluation of postpartum body changes, and perceived sociocultural appearance pressure related to postpartum body changes.
Secondary outcomes will include postnatal depressive and anxiety symptoms, self-compassion, and general health status.
Outcomes will be assessed at baseline, post-intervention, and three-month follow-up.
Analyses will compare changes between the intervention and control groups and examine the maintenance of intervention effects at follow-up for intervention group.

If shown to be effective, BODYPOSI has the potential to improve body image and psychological well-being among postpartum women while supporting the wider implementation of accessible digital interventions in postpartum care.
Research on postpartum body image has received increasing attention in recent years (Lee et al., 2025; Siqueira et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Research on postpartum body image has received increasing attention in recent years <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Lee et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Siqueira et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The postpartum period represents a unique developmental transition characterized by substantial biological, psychological, and social changes as women adapt to motherhood (Hwang et al, 2022).
text.formatted: The postpartum period represents a unique developmental transition characterized by substantial biological, psychological, and social changes as women adapt to motherhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hwang et al, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: During this period, women experience rapid physical changes associated with pregnancy, childbirth, recovery, breastfeeding, and infant care, making body image particularly salient.
Research suggests that body image concerns are common during both pregnancy and the postpartum period.

However, there are no official representative statistics, and prevalence estimates reported across studies vary depending on the populations studied, assessment methods, and definitions of body dissatisfaction.
During pregnancy, body dissatisfaction has been reported in approximately one-third to nearly one-half of women (Roomruangwong et al., 2017; Sui et al., 2013).
text.formatted: During pregnancy, body dissatisfaction has been reported in approximately one-third to nearly one-half of women <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Roomruangwong et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Sui et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Postpartum studies similarly indicate that body image concerns remain prevalent after childbirth. Grajek et al. (2022) found that 68.8% of postpartum women were dissatisfied with their current body weight and figure, while Owusu et al. (2025) reported that only 56.2% of women were satisfied with their bodies after delivery.

text.text: Together, these findings indicate that body image concerns affect a substantial proportion of women during the transition to motherhood and represent an important target for intervention.
Postpartum body dissatisfaction is not only common but also clinically relevant.

Studies have linked negative body image to depressive symptoms (Bakhteh et al., 2023; Kariuki et al., 2022; Schlaff et al., 2020), diagnosis of perinatal depression (He et al., 2025), and disordered eating behaviours (Rodgers et al., 2018).

text.text: Furthermore, body image concerns may extend beyond maternal psychological wellbeing and affect aspects of the mother-infant relationship.
Higher body dissatisfaction has been associated with lower breastfeeding self-efficacy and greater perceived breastfeeding barriers (Kapa et al., 2022; Rodgers et al., 2018).

text.text: These findings suggest that body image concerns may influence not only women's emotional wellbeing but also important health behaviours and early parenting experiences.
Traditionally, body image research has focused on body dissatisfaction and appearance-related distress.

However, contemporary theoretical perspectives conceptualize positive body image as a distinct construct rather than merely the absence of negative body image (Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a; Webb et al., 2015).

text.text: Positive body image encompasses body appreciation, body acceptance, respect for the body's needs, appreciation of body functionality, and the ability to maintain a favourable view of one's body despite sociocultural appearance pressures (Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a).

text.text: Individuals with a positive body image tend to appreciate their bodies for what they can do rather than focusing exclusively on appearance and are better able to resist unrealistic appearance ideals.
This perspective may be particularly relevant during the postpartum period.
Pregnancy, childbirth, breastfeeding, and infant care can substantially alter women's bodies and challenge appearance-based evaluations of self.
At the same time, women are frequently exposed to societal expectations regarding rapid physical recovery and a return to their pre-pregnancy appearance (Liechty et al., 2018).

text.text: Positive body image theory suggests that fostering body appreciation, self-compassion, and appreciation of body functionality may help women adapt more successfully to these changes than approaches focused solely on reducing body dissatisfaction (Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a).

text.text: Indeed, the postpartum body is not only an object of appearance but also a body that has undergone pregnancy and childbirth and may be nourishing and caring for an infant.

Consequently, interventions that encourage women to appreciate their bodies' capabilities, resilience, and functionality may be particularly beneficial during this life stage (Alleva et al., 2015; Cerea et al., 2024).

text.text: However, postpartum body image is influenced by a range of relational, psychological, and sociocultural factors.
A recent systematic review (Siqueira et al., 2025) identified sociocultural influences, social support, and breastfeeding as key determinants of postpartum body dissatisfaction.

text.text: In addition, regression analyses included in the review identified maternal weight, depressive symptoms, maternal age, mode of delivery, and sexual functioning as significant correlates of postpartum body dissatisfaction.
Among these factors, sociocultural influences appear to play a particularly important role.

Postpartum body dissatisfaction has been associated with perceived appearance pressure from partners, friends, and the media, with these associations often mediated by the internalization of the thin ideal (Lovering et al., 2018).

text.text: Similarly, greater internalization of appearance ideals and partner appearance pressure have been associated with higher body dissatisfaction among postpartum women (Rodgers et al., 2022).

text.text: In contrast, greater self-compassion, defined as an attitude of kindness and understanding toward one's own difficulties, encompassing mindfulness, selfkindness, and common humanity (Neff, 2003), has consistently been associated with more positive body image (Turk & Waller, 2020).

text.text: Together, these findings highlight the need for interventions that not only address body dissatisfaction but also strengthen women's ability to resist unrealistic appearance expectations, cultivate self-compassion, and develop a more positive relationship with their postpartum bodies.
Evidence suggests that psychological interventions can improve body image and related outcomes during the postpartum period.

A recent systematic scoping review found beneficial effects of cognitive-behavioural, mindfulness-, and self-compassion-based interventions delivered both face-to-face and through digital platforms (Blinded for per-review, 2026).
These interventions improved body image, body appreciation, self-esteem, sexual satisfaction, and body-related distress.

Digital delivery formats, including websites, mobile applications, and social media-based programmes, appeared particularly promising because they offer flexibility and accessibility for mothers who may face time, transportation, and childcare constraints.
providing women with access to information, support, and experiences shared by other mothers, thereby fostering a sense of connectedness during the postpartum period.
Despite these encouraging findings, the review also identified several important gaps (Blinded for per-review, 2026).
Existing interventions vary considerably in their theoretical foundations and intervention components.

Most were based on cognitive-behavioural, mindfulness, selfcompassion, or psychoeducational approaches, whereas only one intervention was explicitly developed within a positive body image framework (Becker et al., 2022) and another incorporated selected positive body image elements within a broader self-compassion intervention (Papini et al., 2022).

text.text: Consequently, interventions specifically targeting core positive body image constructs, such as body appreciation, body functionality, and resistance to sociocultural appearance pressures, remain scarce in the postpartum literature.
Furthermore, evidence regarding long-term effectiveness remains limited.
These findings highlight the need for theory-driven interventions that explicitly promote positive body image and can be delivered in an accessible format to postpartum women.

To address these gaps, we developed the Positive Body Image Digital Self-Help Programme (BODYPOSI), an online intervention grounded in positive body image theory and informed by evidence-based approaches, including self-compassion, appreciation of body functionality, and resistance to unrealistic appearance ideals.
Delivered through a digital self-help format, BODYPOSI aims to provide flexible and accessible support for postpartum women while accommodating the practical demands of early motherhood.

The present RCT intends to test the developed online self-help intervention BODYPOSI, which applies concepts of positive body image theory (Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a) as the programme's theoretical framework.

text.text: The main aim of the study is to evaluate whether the BODYPOSI intervention improves the positive body image of postpartum women, and whether these effects are maintained at the three-month follow-up.
The study will also examine whether improvements in positive body image mediate the effects of the intervention on psychological wellbeing.
The following research questions are addressed: 1.
Do participants in the BODYPOSI intervention show greater improvements in body image outcomes than those in the waitlist control group?
Do participants in the BODYPOSI intervention show greater reductions in perceived sociocultural pressure related to postpartum body changes than those in the waitlist control group?

Are improvements in body image outcomes and reductions in perceived sociocultural appearance pressure among participants in the BODYPOSI intervention maintained from the end of the intervention to the 3-month follow-up?

Do participants in the BODYPOSI intervention show greater improvements in secondary outcomes, including postnatal depressive symptoms, postpartum-specific anxiety, selfcompassion, and general health status, than those in the waitlist control group?
Do improvements in body image outcomes mediate the effects of the BODYPOSI intervention on psychological well-being?
The study is designed as a two-arm RCT comparing the intervention group with a waitlist control group across baseline and immediate post-intervention assessment.

Participants will be eligible if they are between 6 weeks and 12 months of postpartum and do not report having an eating disorder or other medical conditions that could substantially affect their body image perception.
Participants assigned to the intervention condition will have immediate access to a four-week online positive body image self-help programme designed for women in the postpartum period.
Participants in the waitlist control condition will receive access to the programme after four weeks, when the post-intervention assessment for both groups is completed.
The intervention will be delivered through an online platform enabling participants to access the program remotely from any location with internet access.
Outcomes will be measured at three time points for the intervention group: baseline before randomisation (T0), immediately after the intervention (T1), and three months after the intervention (T2).
Participants in the waitlist control group will complete assessments at T0 and T1.
After this, they will receive access to the programme (Figure 1).

text.text: Participants will be recruited online through social media groups and online communities for postpartum women, media dissemination, as well as collaborations with public figures and organisations that discuss postpartum well-being, perinatal mental health, motherhood, and body image.
Interested women will be directed to the study website, where they will receive detailed information about the programme and study procedures.
After creating an account on the study platform and providing electronic informed consent, participants will complete eligibility screening and baseline assessment.

Once T0 is completed, participants will be randomly assigned to either the intervention group or the waitlist control group using an automated randomisation algorithm integrated into the online platform.
Due to the nature of the intervention, participant blinding will not be possible.

text.text: The T0 assessment includes sociodemographic characteristics (mother's and child's age, place of residence, marital status, education, income, and number of children), physical characteristics (height, current weight, pre-pregnancy weight, and general health), and pregnancy and birth characteristics, including pregnancy intention, gestational week, birth mode, birth plurality, maternal complications, and breastfeeding status.
In addition, participants at T0 will complete all primary and secondary outcome measures included in the study.
The T1 and T2 assessments include repeated assessments of all primary and secondary outcome measures, as well as updated information on current weight.
At T1, participants will also provide feedback on the programme, including its acceptability, perceived benefits, and their subjective experience.
At T2, participants in the intervention group will additionally report whether they continued using the programme after its completion and, if so, how frequently.

text.text: Effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals will also be reported.
The primary intervention effect will be evaluated using linear mixed-effects models comparing the intervention and waitlist control groups from T0 to T1.
These models will include time, group, and the group × time interaction as fixed effects, with a random intercept for participants to account for repeated measurements.
The group × time interaction will be considered the main indicator of intervention efficacy.
Estimated marginal means will be used to examine within-and between-group differences, and Bonferroni correction will be applied for multiple comparisons.
The maintenance of intervention effects within the intervention group will be examined using linear mixed-effects models, which will include T0, T1, and T2 assessments.
Time will be included as a fixed effect, with a random intercept for participants.
Planned pairwise comparisons will be conducted to evaluate changes from T0 to T1, from T1 to T2, and from T0 to T2.
Bonferroni correction will be applied to control for multiple testing.

In addition, exploratory analyses will be conducted to examine whether changes in positive body image are associated with changes in postnatal depressive symptoms, postpartum anxiety, self-compassion, and general health status over time.
If adequately powered, mediation analyses will be conducted to examine whether improvements in positive body image mediate the effects of the intervention on psychological outcomes.

The intervention is grounded in the conceptual framework of positive body image proposed by Tylka and Wood-Barcalow (2015a).

text.text: According to this framework, positive body image is conceptualized not merely as the absence of body dissatisfaction, but as a distinct and multifaceted construct characterised by body appreciation, body acceptance and love, broad conceptualizations of beauty, adaptive appearance investment, inner positivity, and the ability to interpret appearance-related information in a body-protective manner.

The framework emphasises the appreciation of the body's functionality and uniqueness, the engagement in self-care behaviours, and the development of a compassionate and accepting relationship with the body despite sociocultural appearance pressures.

It also highlights the importance of protective psychological processes, such as resisting unrealistic appearance ideals and critically evaluating appearance-related messages (Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a).
text.formatted: It also highlights the importance of protective psychological processes, such as resisting unrealistic appearance ideals and critically evaluating appearance-related messages <ref type="bibr">(Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a)</ref>.

text.text: This approach may be particularly relevant for postpartum women, who often experience substantial bodily changes alongside sociocultural and self-imposed pressures to rapidly return to their pre-pregnancy appearance following childbirth.
Given the multidimensional nature of positive body image, the intervention was designed to target the cognitive, emotional, behavioural, and reflective processes related to body image.
To achieve this, the programme incorporates multiple approaches, including psychoeducation, reflective writing, mindfulness-based activities, and self-compassion exercises.

Previous research on body image interventions suggests that combining diverse approaches may help address multiple aspects of body image simultaneously while also enhancing engagement and acceptability of digital formats (Guest et al., 2019; Conboy et al., 2024).

text.text: Initially, 22 tasks targeting different components of positive body image were developed by the study authors using a variety of task approaches.
The tasks were discussed and refined to improve the clarity, diversity, logical structure, and sensitivity of the content.
Subsequently, 12 tasks were selected based on their ability to cover the key components of positive body image, while maintaining diversity of activities and clear instructions.

The order of the tasks was determined through discussions among the study authors, taking into account the logical progression of content, task depth, and the sensitivity for participants without prior knowledge of positive body image concepts.
BODYPOSI was developed to address the limited availability of positive body image interventions specifically tailored for postpartum women (Blinded for per-review, 2026).
It is a four-week digital self-help intervention consisting of 12 tasks, which are delivered through an online platform, with participants completing three tasks per week.
The programme includes psychoeducational, reflective, and experiential activities aimed at promoting a positive body image during the postpartum period.

The tasks are organised in a gradual, logical sequence, beginning with psychoeducation and body image awareness and progressing toward deeper reflection, body acceptance, and the long-term maintenance of positive body image practices.

Participants read psychoeducational material about positive body image after childbirth and then complete a short knowledge test.
Body acceptance and appreciation
Participants are asked to complete a reflective writing task.
First, they recall three meaningful life events that made them feel proud of their body.
Then, they write down three aspects of their body that they value based on its functionality rather than appearance.
Participants are asked to focus on their body, notice its sensations, reflect in writing on its needs, and choose and engage in an activity that provides care, comfort, or pleasure for their body.

Participants are asked to read psychoeducational material on self-acceptance and flexibility in body image and complete a short knowledge test.

They are then asked to briefly reflect on their experience in writing.
Participants are asked to identify personal values relating to their body, reflect on how these values are expressed in their life, and formulate a positive statement about their body.
They are then encouraged to display the statement somewhere visible and refer to it during moments of selfcriticism or doubt about their body.
Participants are asked to reflect on factors that negatively influence their body image, and to write down at least three actions they can take to protect and strengthen it.
Next, they are asked to write a gratitude letter to their body, focusing on what their body can do and expressing appreciation for what it has done for them today.

Participants are asked to observe their body in a mirror without judgment, select a body part that they find difficult to accept, and express appreciation or gratitude towards it.
They are then asked to write a brief reflection.

Next, they engage in a self-care activity focused on the same body part (e.g., massage, stretching, warm shower) while attending to bodily sensations and expressing appreciation for the body's functions.

Self-and body acceptance mindfulness-based meditation Participants are asked to complete a guided mindfulnessbased meditation aimed at promoting relaxation and acceptance of the self and body, followed by reflection on their experience.

Participants are asked to review psychoeducational content and practical advice on maintaining a positive body image, and to apply practical strategies (e.g., self-compassion, focusing on body functionality, mindful social media use, and revisiting previously learned exercises).
These strategies are intended to support the long-term maintenance of a positive body image.
Finally, they are asked to reflect on how their participation in the programme has changed their body image perception.

Initial testing of the programme's technical functionality, clarity of instructions, logical structure, questionnaire accuracy, and overall usability was conducted with eight Health Psychology Master's students using a structured online questionnaire containing open-ended questions.

The feedback indicated that the registration process was straightforward, the instructions and order of tasks were logical and easy to follow, and the content was engaging, clear, and acceptable overall.
Based on participants' feedback, several revisions were made to the programme.
These mainly involved correcting typographical errors in the questionnaire items and standardizing font sizes to improve the programme's visual clarity.
Following the programme revisions, a pilot experimental study was conducted with 10 postpartum women using the same procedures planned for the main trial.
Participants completed the baseline assessment (T0), the 4-week intervention, and the post-intervention assessment (T1).

Following completion of the intervention, they participated in individual semi-structured interviews to explore their experiences with the programme, including its acceptability, perceived benefits, organisation, and questionnaire burden.
The interviews were conducted via Microsoft Teams or Zoom, audio-recorded, and transcribed verbatim.

The data were analysed using thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2022), guided by the key domains of intervention feasibility proposed by Bowen et al. (2009), to identify recurring patterns in participants' experiences.

text.text: Overall, participants perceived the programme as feasible, acceptable, and relevant.
They also reported that the questionnaires did not impose a significant burden and that the intervention promoted greater awareness and acceptance of postpartum body changes.

The qualitative interviews identified three main themes: (1) perceived improvements in body image and acceptance of postpartum body changes, (2) positive experiences with specific intervention components, particularly body functionality and mindfulness exercises, and (3) suggestions to improve the programme's flexibility and usability.

A recurring theme was that the programme encouraged participants to shift their attention from appearance-related concerns towards appreciation of their body's functionality and achievements during pregnancy and childbirth.

One participant reflected: Other participants noted that restrictions on task completion, such as the automatic closure of weekly modules, reduced flexibility because they were sometimes unable to submit tasks or complete all programme activities.
They suggested that allowing multiple tasks to be completed in one day and providing additional reminders would improve engagement and task completion.
Based on these findings, the programme was refined before the main trial.

The revisions included redefining Week 1 to begin with the first completed task, adding a weekly countdown timer, removing the one-task-per-day limit while retaining the three-tasks-per-week cap, and improving reminder messages and access links to enhance clarity, usability, and participant engagement.
The BODYPOSI study was developed to address several important gaps in the existing literature on postpartum body image interventions.

Despite growing recognition of the importance of positive body image during the perinatal period, relatively few interventions have explicitly targeted positive body image constructs, and even fewer have adopted a comprehensive approach encompassing multiple dimensions of positive body image.
Furthermore, accessible interventions that can be integrated into the time constraints and responsibilities of early motherhood remain limited.

The present study will evaluate the effectiveness of a brief digital self-help programme designed to promote positive body image while also examining its potential effects on broader psychological well-being.

If effective, the BODYPOSI programme may provide an accessible, low-cost intervention that could be incorporated into routine postpartum care to support women's body image and psychological well-being.
This study has several important strengths.
First, the use of a randomised controlled trial design with a waitlist control group provides a rigorous approach for evaluating the efficacy of a psychological intervention.

Random allocation helps minimise selection bias and reduces the likelihood that observed differences between groups reflect pre-existing differences in motivation, symptom severity, or other confounding variables.

Second, the BODYPOSI programme was developed based on contemporary theoretical and empirical evidence on positive body image and integrates multiple evidence-informed techniques targeting complementary mechanisms involved in postpartum body image adaptation, including body functionality appreciation, self-compassion, mindfulness, and reduction of sociocultural appearance pressures.
This multidimensional approach addresses several components of positive body image rather than focusing on a single mechanism of change.
Third, the internetbased delivery format offers substantial practical advantages.
It enables women to participate from home at times convenient to them, which is particularly important for postpartum women who face significant time constraints due to infant care responsibilities.
It also reduces barriers to recruitment and retention commonly encountered in clinic-based postpartum research, such as travel, childcare needs, and scheduling conflicts.
Finally, the inclusion of a three-month follow-up assessment allows evaluation of the durability of treatment effects beyond immediate post-intervention improvements.
Nevertheless, several limitations should be acknowledged.

Although the use of a waitlist control group is ethically appropriate given the absence of an established evidence-based intervention for promoting positive body image in postpartum women, it does not control for non-specific intervention effects, such as participants' expectations or the additional attention associated with receiving an intervention.

Consequently, while the study will determine whether the BODYPOSI programme is more effective than no intervention, it will not be possible to determine the extent to which the observed effects are attributable to the programme's specific therapeutic components rather than to these non-specific factors.

Moreover, the exclusion of women with diagnosed eating disorders, while methodologically prudent to ensure participant safety and avoid confounding with a distinct clinical condition, limits the generalisability of the findings.
Many postpartum women experience subclinical eating disorder symptoms or disordered eating behaviours that may respond differently to the intervention.
Additionally, recruitment is likely to attract women who are motivated to improve their body image and who have adequate internet access and digital literacy.

Although the recruitment materials invite all eligible postpartum women to participate and emphasise contributing to the evaluation of the programme rather than only seeking help for body image concerns, some degree of self-selection bias is unavoidable and may limit the representativeness of the study sample.

Lastly, the 4-week duration of the intervention and the requirement to complete three short tasks per week may contribute to participant attrition, particularly among women experiencing high infant care demands, sleep deprivation, or postpartum mood difficulties.
Although attrition rates will be monitored and reported transparently, differential dropout between groups could bias effect estimates.
Primary analyses will follow the intention-to-treat principle, with all randomised participants included using appropriate methods to account for missing outcome data.

Despite these limitations, the BODYPOSI trial has the potential to provide important evidence regarding the efficacy of a brief, internet-based positive body image self-help programme for postpartum women.

If effective, the BODYPOSI programme may offer an accessible and lowcost approach to promoting positive body image and psychological well-being among postpartum women and provide a foundation for larger-scale effectiveness studies and future implementation in postnatal care.

(V.) Participants also described becoming more accepting of the natural variability of postpartum body recovery and feeling less pressure to compare themselves with others: "I simply realized after your program that everything happens in its own time, and there's really no need to pressure yourself into certain standards.
Just because, for example, someone else has a flat stomach after giving birth doesn't mean that I have to be the same, because everybody truly responds differently."

(M.) Several participants highlighted individual intervention activities as particularly meaningful, especially exercises focusing on body functionality and gratitude towards one's body: "I think thanking my hands was something I did for the first time.
I really paid attention to them and thought… they actually do so much, holding my baby, caressing them, taking care of everything.
I realized I had never thanked my hands before.
That was a really meaningful moment for me, and it has stayed with me."
(E.) Participants also suggested several improvements to the programme's organisation to better accommodate the routines of new mothers.
A recurring challenge was remembering to complete the weekly tasks and finding sufficient time and opportunity to participate fully in the intervention.
One participant explained: "I did most of those tasks while my daughter was nearby, dozing off or asleep...
When there was an audio recording, I had to turn it off because I didn't have headphones.
Then I didn't get around to the task, and it just ended up not getting done.
That's when I realised I needed better conditions: silence, peace, and maybe some additional tools."
